question: Didier Reynders, a former Belgian minister and the European Commissioner for Justice until 2024, stands accused of money laundering. The investigation focuses on 245 suspicious deposits of cash into his accounts, amounting to EUR 836 500, and 779 purchases of National Lottery tickets at a petrol station, totalling around EUR 202 491 (with individual bets sometimes reaching EUR 2 000 to EUR 3 000)1.

Altogether, those figures amount to over EUR 1 million. Ironically, the Commissioner had been responsible for the new anti-money laundering legislation. On 10 June 2026, the Commission confirmed that it had ‘not conducted any internal investigations following the allegations’2. On 5 February 2026, it stated that it had ‘not been involved in any investigations’3. In view of the seriousness of the allegations: 1.

Has it requested or received additional information from the Belgian judicial authorities about the origin of the money flows, the services provided and any people or entities potentially behind the money laundering?
Will the Commission’s new anti-fraud architecture provide for systematic internal investigations when commissioners are involved in financial scandals?
